title: Containers and Container Images
description: Learn what containers are, how they differ from virtual machines, and why container images are the standard way to package applications.

data.text: A container is a lightweight, standalone package containing everything an application needs to run: code, runtime, system tools, libraries, and settings. Containers run consistently across any environment that supports the container runtime.

cards.title: Virtual Machine
cards.description: A full operating system running on a hypervisor.

cards.title: Container
cards.description: An isolated process sharing the host OS kernel.

data.text: A container image is a read-only template that defines how a container runs. It includes the application code, dependencies, and configuration. Images are stored in registries and versioned with tags.

items: Container: A running instance of an image
Registry: Storage service for images (Docker Hub, ACR)
Tag: A label for a specific version (e.g. 'latest', 'v1.2')

data.title: Portability
data.text: Containers run the same way on your laptop, on-premises servers, and in any cloud provider. Build once, run anywhere.

terms.definition: A running instance of a container image, isolated from other processes on the host.
A read-only, layered package that defines how a container runs, including code and dependencies.
A storage and distribution service for container images, such as Docker Hub or Azure Container Registry.
A human-readable label that identifies a specific version of a container image.

data.text: A multi-stage Dockerfile builds the application in a large SDK image and copies only the published output into a smaller runtime image. That keeps the final image small and removes the compiler and source code from production.

data.title: Multi-stage Dockerfile for an ASP.NET Core API
data.content: The build stage restores packages first so Docker can cache that layer when only source files change.
data.code:
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:8.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY *.csproj ./
RUN dotnet restore
COPY . .
RUN dotnet publish -c Release -o /app/publish /p:UseAppHost=false

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0 AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/publish .
EXPOSE 8080
ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "Demo.Api.dll"]

data.title: Build, run, and push to Azure Container Registry
data.content: The local run proves the image works before it reaches a registry. The tag includes a version so deployments are reproducible.
data.code:
docker build -t demo-api:1.0 .
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 demo-api:1.0

az acr login --name myregistry
docker tag demo-api:1.0 myregistry.azurecr.io/demo-api:1.0
docker push myregistry.azurecr.io/demo-api:1.0

data.title: Tags are mutable; digests are not
data.text: Pushing `demo-api:latest` twice silently replaces the image that the tag points to, which makes rollbacks and audits unreliable. Use a version or git SHA as the tag, or deploy by image digest. Also keep the base image patched: rebuild regularly so the runtime image picks up security fixes.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Containers package apps with all dependencies
Containers are more lightweight than VMs
Images are stored in registries and versioned with tags
data.takeaway: Containers provide consistent, portable application packaging.
